title: Henry Hub averaged $2.93 this summer, 6% below 2025, despite the warmest July on record
summary: EIA reports that the Henry Hub natural gas spot price averaged $2.93 per million British thermal units from June through August 2026, 6 percent less than a year earlier, even though July was the warmest July on record for the Lower 48. It points to more solar and wind generation, record production, ample storage and maintenance at LNG terminals.

source.title: Today in Energy: Henry Hub natural gas prices this summer were 6% lower than last summer
source.timezone_note: The article page states a date only. No time or time zone is stated, so none is recorded and the date is not converted.
source.reference_period: June through August 2026, compared with the same months of 2025

overview: Natural gas prices fell year on year through a very hot summer. The Henry Hub spot price averaged $2.93 per million British thermal units (MMBtu) from June through August 2026, 6 percent less than in the same months of 2025. EIA notes that July's average Lower 48 temperature of 77°F was the warmest on record for the month, according to NOAA data.

EIA attributes the lower prices to supply, and to less gas being burned for power than the heat alone would imply. Solar generation rose an estimated 19.4 billion kilowatthours and wind 9.3 billion compared with the same months of 2025, while gas-fired generation rose 7.5 billion. Production was an estimated 2 percent (2.7 billion cubic feet per day) higher than a year earlier, and EIA's September Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO) expects a record 111.2 Bcf/d of dry gas production in 2026. Maintenance at liquefied natural gas terminals also moderated demand growth.

Storage provided a cushion. Working gas entered the April injection season at 1,906 billion cubic feet, 4 percent above the previous five-year average, and monthly injections exceeded their five-year averages in every month through August except May. EIA's August STEO forecast Lower 48 inventories of 3,985 Bcf at the end of October, 5 percent above the five-year average.

channels.title: Gas burned for power, and gas prices
channels.source_fact: Solar (+19.4 BkWh) and wind (+9.3 BkWh) rose more than gas-fired generation (+7.5 BkWh) in a record-hot summer.
channels.interpretation: If renewable additions keep absorbing part of peak summer demand, hot weather would raise gas burn less than in past summers, damping one way heat lifts gas prices. One summer is not enough to judge how stable that offset is.

channels.title: Storage cushion for the winter (gas buyers and utilities)
channels.source_fact: Record production and end-October inventories forecast 5% above the five-year average.
channels.interpretation: Ample storage going into winter would, other things equal, limit upward price pressure in the heating season; a colder-than-normal winter or higher LNG feedgas demand could still tighten supply. The article does not forecast winter prices.

channels.title: Producer revenue (natural gas producers)
channels.source_fact: Prices 6% lower year on year while production was 2% higher.
channels.interpretation: Lower prices with somewhat higher volumes imply flat to lower gas sales revenue for producers in aggregate, depending on hedging and regional prices. This is arithmetic on the stated figures, not a reported revenue number.

competing_explanations.title: LNG maintenance as a temporary factor
competing_explanations.detail: EIA notes that maintenance at LNG terminals moderated demand growth. If export demand returned once maintenance ended, part of the summer's price weakness would reflect a temporary pause rather than lasting abundance.

competing_explanations.title: Heat across the whole summer
competing_explanations.detail: The article reports the warmest July but not cooling degree days or weather-adjusted demand for June through August. If June and August were less extreme, 'despite exceptionally hot weather' may overstate the demand shock over the three months.

assumptions: Henry Hub spot prices stand for US natural gas prices generally; regional prices can diverge from Henry Hub.
The generation and production figures are EIA estimates and forecasts from different STEO editions, and they may be revised.
missing_information: Futures prices or a sourced expectation for summer prices; without them the case cannot say whether lower prices were a surprise.
Cooling degree days or weather-adjusted demand for June through August.
LNG feedgas volumes and how long the terminal maintenance lasted.
The September STEO's storage forecast; the article cites the August STEO for end-October inventories.
weakening_observations: If end-October inventories came in well below 3,985 Bcf, the storage-cushion reading would weaken.
If later STEO revisions cut the 19.4 BkWh solar estimate substantially, the renewables explanation would carry less weight.
If LNG feedgas demand rebounded sharply after maintenance and prices rose, the temporary-factor explanation would gain over the abundance reading.

critique.title: Two outlook editions in one argument
critique.detail: The production forecast comes from the September STEO and the storage forecast from the August STEO. Mixing editions is common in a short article, but it means the supply picture combines estimates of different vintages.

critique.title: Attribution without a breakdown
critique.detail: EIA lists renewables, production, storage and LNG maintenance as reasons but gives no breakdown of how much each lowered prices. The channels therefore stay qualitative; ranking them would go beyond the source.

critique.title: A year-on-year frame
critique.detail: A 6% decline compares two summers. It does not say whether prices were low relative to costs or to expectations, so the case avoids calling them weak or surprising.
